articleTitle: Modern materials technologies in PCB thermal management
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on CAD (Computer Aided Design) Tools for Thermal Management (Digest No.027)
abstract: Development of faster and more powerful components, along with increasing component density on a PCB, has led to an increase in the power consumption per square inch of PCBs. Any increase in power consumption also leads to an increase in the amount of heat being produced. The necessity for thermal management has been shown by this paper as something that needs to be accessed at the early stages of design. Forward thinking as to how hot and where heat will be concentrated during a system's life is a primary concern for reliable service. The design example shown has processing components sited at the centre of the PCB surrounded by cooler memory component. If thought was given towards thermal management at the initial design stage, then the board may have been designated to run cooler if the 'hotter' processing components had been sited closer towards the cold walls as this would dissipate heat more efficiently.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Thermal modelling of solder joint formation
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on CAD (Computer Aided Design) Tools for Thermal Management (Digest No.027)
abstract: The use of low-power lasers as an energy source for the purposes of soldering has many advantages. With limited laser power, the creation of a successful solder joint is strongly dependent on controlling and identifying any heat losses. The combination of experimental and theoretical work has identified the importance of: (1) substrate properties: in particular, changing the thermal conductivity can lead to substantial differences in the melting characteristics; (2) the layout of copper tracking: the enhanced sink effect can be very deleterious; and (3) accurate modelling of heat losses to the environment in any theoretical analysis.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of CFD software to solving air flow and heat transfer in power supplies
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on CAD (Computer Aided Design) Tools for Thermal Management (Digest No.027)
abstract: Describes the use of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) by ERA Technology Ltd. to investigate heat transfer and airflow in electronic systems. Because computing time is the limiting factor in simulating most real problems, techniques for simplifying the representations are described. This is followed by an example which shows that, with the simplifying assumptions used, accurate results may still be obtained.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A process model of the infra-red reflow soldering of printed circuit assemblies
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on CAD (Computer Aided Design) Tools for Thermal Management (Digest No.027)
abstract: Outlines the results of a major project to demonstrate the pre-production simulation of thermal processes used in the assembly of printed circuit boards. A study of the limitations of this project is also summarised. These limitations have allowed the definition of a further project which aims to produce a more complete modelling tool supported by sufficient experimentally gathered process data to allow confident interpretation of the modelling results.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The development of fast, thermal-analyses tools for CAD and further practical applications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on CAD (Computer Aided Design) Tools for Thermal Management (Digest No.027)
abstract: A suite of computer programs has been developed and integrated to comprise a user-friendly thermal template. This design tool has been successfully employed to model the thermal behaviour, including stress and strain distributions, of printed circuit boards, pressed contacts, electrical rotating machines and thermally-insulated district-heating pipelines. The output is such that either graphical interpretations are readily presented, in 2D or 3D, or further statistical manipulation is easily initiated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Heat transfer in windings: CAD techniques for thermal management
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on CAD (Computer Aided Design) Tools for Thermal Management (Digest No.027)
abstract: Heat transfer within and from windings has been analysed using dimensionless constants and spreadsheet calculations. This has enabled predictions of thermal behaviour when changes in the geometry or number of conductors in a group alters. The effects of air voids and layers, coatings and insulation, material degradation and consequences of parallel and perpendicular conduction can also be analysed. The results are compared with those obtained using more sophisticated CAD tools.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Simulating the behaviour of ceramics during firing
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on CAD (Computer Aided Design) Tools for Thermal Management (Digest No.027)
abstract: The details of the temperature fields within a piece of ceramic during firing and their variation with time has a significant influence on the yield of the firing process. Inappropriate firing can result in the creation of local defects or in atypical deformation of the piece as a whole. The thermal effects within a piece of ceramic are, in turn, related to the conditions existing in the kiln and to the position of the body of interest within the kiln. The authors describe a model of the thermal effects within a piece of ceramic during firing in a tunnel kiln. The thermal model is coupled to a model of deformation, to allow final geometry to be predicted.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
